catalog_quote: This chapter is a sketch of the tonal system of the Ambele language. It will therefore provide an inventory of the tones, discuss the phonemic status of level tones, give tone patterns and some tonal processes that are attested within words. ... Ambele is a tone language. That is one which uses tones to distinguish meaning. According to Pike (1945), a tone language is that which has lexically significant, contrastive but relative pitch on each syllable. Therefore, any change in the syllable pitch leads to a change in the meaning of this syllable or word. The Ambele language has three phonemic tones: the high, mid and low tones (H, M.L). Contour tones in this language are derived from floating tones docking onto the adjacent tone bearing unit (TBU). These floating tones result from vowel deletion (4.1.1) or from vowels which devocalise into glides (4.1.4).
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only description treats Ambele as a three-level tone language (H, M, L phonemic; falling/rising contours derived from glide formation and vowel deletion) and makes no statement of any kind about word stress or accent; no stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress discussion). Tonal processes described: tone docking, tone fusion, regressive tone spreading, Meeussen's rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone described at word level (tone patterns by mono-/di-/tri-/quadrisyllabic words, section 5.4); nothing on phrase-level prominence or intonation.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Ambele (autonym given for the language, spoken by the Ambele clan, Widikum subdivision, Momo Division, NW Cameroon) = ambe1247 exactly; principal consultant named (Egbe Vallynash); no dialect subdivision discussed.
